questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a First-Order Inhomogeneous ODE With Polynomial Forcing
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+7y=14.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-7x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}+7{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-7x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\beta 
$$

where $\beta $ is a constant to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=0.
$$

To find the value of $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
0+7\beta =14
$$

Solving this equation gives $\beta =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=2.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-7x}+2.
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following recurrence relations are first-order?

- ${a}_{n}=4{a}_{n-1}+7$
- ${b}_{n}={b}_{n-1}+3{b}_{n-3}$
- ${c}_{n}=5{c}_{n-1}-2n$
questions.worked_solution:
The order of a recurrence relation is the largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding terms in the relation.

Let's examine each recurrence relation in turn.

- The largest index difference between ${a}_{n}$ and the preceding term ${a}_{n-1}$ in the relation is $1.$ So, this recurrence relation has order $1.$

- The largest index difference between ${b}_{n}$ and the preceding terms ${b}_{n-1}$ and ${b}_{n-3}$ in the relation is $3.$ So, this recurrence relation has order $3.$

- The largest index difference between ${c}_{n}$ and the preceding term ${c}_{n-1}$ in the relation is $1.$ So, this recurrence relation has order $1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Norm of a Vector in an Inner Product Space of Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Let $V=C[-\pi ,\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }x(t)y(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The norm of a vector $f(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
‖f(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨f(t),f(t)⟩}.
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(t),f(t)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(f(t))^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\,{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{4}){|}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{4})-(-\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )}{4}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we made use of the trigonometric identity 

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡t=\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖f(t)‖ & =\sqrt{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Linear System of Differential Equations in Matrix Form
questions.problem:
If the following system of differential equations is written in the form ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then what is the matrix $A?$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+7{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)+4{x}_{1}(t)-8{x}_{2}(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables).

Such a system can always be written in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

where

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a(t) & b(t) \\ c(t) & d(t)\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}f(t) \\ g(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

We have the following system.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)+7{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)=0 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)+4{x}_{1}(t)-8{x}_{2}(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-7{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-4{x}_{1}(t)+8{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can rewrite our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

provenance.kp_title: Writing a Linear System of Differential Equations in Matrix Form

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Differential Operators With Functions of X as Coefficients
questions.worked_solution:
The given operator is a third-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y.
$$

with ${f}_{3}={x}^{2},{f}_{2}=3x,{f}_{1}=-1,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x})(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}(\frac{1}{x})+3x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{x})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})+3x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})-(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+3x(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{6}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Applying Differential Operators With Functions of X as Coefficients

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14093248/assets/f915caf118419deb78dc0b34f9bba0a977c01989c08a632fb2ae39b669f070e7.png)

The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14093248/assets/26137173c268215296020c7768cf43748b1c3fcdc06d73fe1f3ecfda7f515d58.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=-3$ and $y=1.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(y+3)(1-y) \\ {y}^{′} & =-(y+3)(y-1)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =y(y+3)(y-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We can dismiss the equation ${y}^{′}=y(y+3)(y-1).$ Although the right-hand side evaluates to zero at $y=-3$ and $y=1,$ it also evaluates to zero when $y=0,$ which is behavior not exhibited by our slope field.

- Second, the lines $y=-3$ and $y=1$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-3$ | $-3<y<1$ | $y>1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=(y+3)(1-y).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=(y+3)(1-y).$

provenance.kp_title: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes
